# Constants for the centered-layer affine-frustum ansatz in every dimension

This proves only the constant range of the proposed common-c dual. It does not prove that dual for arbitrary centered mixtures.

Let d>=2, H>0, B=H+1, and r(z)=(H-z)/B on the cone interval[-1,H]. Let s*>1 be a finite positive slope whose actual section moment M(s*) is zero. Use the cone notation

    p0=(H/B)^d,
    v*=(s*+1)/(2s*),
    e*=C(s*)/C(0).

For any frustum cutoff parameter T>=s* put

    t=[H/(B+T)]^d,
    beta(t)=(v*-t e*)/[(1-t)(1+e*)].

Then

    4/9 <= beta(t) <= 1/2.

The lower bound follows from the already proved affine-cone energy inequality; the upper bound below supplies a separate geometric check on the truncation correction in arbitrary dimension.

## 1. Lower bound and monotonicity

The centered uniform base layer is a special case of the cone-law theorem, so

    2v*-1 <= e* <= (2v*-1)/v*.

Since (2v*-1)/v*<=v*, we have e*<=v*. Also

    beta(0)=v*/(1+e*) >= (v*)^2/(3v*-1) >=4/9.

Finally

    beta(t)-beta(0)
       =t(v*-e*)/[(1-t)(1+e*)] >=0,

and beta is nondecreasing in t. Thus it remains to prove beta(t*)<=1/2 at

    t*=[H/(B+s*)]^d,

the largest permitted t.

## 2. A decreasing density with mean zero has at most half its mass to the right

Let f be a positive continuous nonincreasing density on a compact interval, normalized to total mass one, with mean zero. Its cumulative distribution F is increasing and concave. Its continuous inverse Q is convex: concavity of F applied at Q(a),Q(b) implies Q((1-lambda)a+lambda b)<= (1-lambda)Q(a)+lambda Q(b). The quantile integration identity gives integral_0^1 Q(v)dv=0. Jensen therefore gives Q(1/2)<=0, so F(0)>=1/2.

If this density is then multiplied by another positive nonincreasing function r and renormalized, its right-of-zero probability can only decrease. Indeed the conditional mean of r on the right is no greater than its conditional mean on the left, and substituting these two conditional means into the normalized right mass proves the claim. This also follows directly by expanding the corresponding cross-multiplied double integral.

## 3. Apply the median fact to the full section

Choose the physical top cutoff

    U*=H s*/(B+s*),

so that U*/r(U*)=s*. The section at slope s* spans the whole interval[-1,U*]: its left end is on the lower axial end, and its right end is on the truncated upper end. Its moment-zero condition is exactly

    integral_-1^U* z r(z)^(d-2) dz=0.

The density r^(d-2) is positive continuous and nonincreasing. Section2 shows that at most half its mass lies at z>=0. The actual axial volume density is r^(d-1), obtained by multiplying by the decreasing r. Hence the horizontal upper cap of this frustum has at most half its volume.

Writing this last statement in the physical cone records yields

    (p0-t*)/(1-t*) <=1/2,
    2p0<=1+t*.                                      (1)

No change of measure is being made in the final statement: the auxiliary section density and the actual volume density are explicitly different, and their comparison is justified by the monotone tilt.

At slope s*, the full-section cap identity is P_frustum=V_frustum/2+M=V_frustum/2. The cone-to-frustum subtraction is exact, so

    p0 e*+1-v*-t*=(1-t*)/2,
    2v*-1=2p0 e*-t*.                                (2)

Combining (1)-(2) gives

    2v*-1-e*+t*(1-e*)=e*(2p0-1-t*)<=0.

This is precisely beta(t*)<=1/2 after multiplying by its positive denominator. Monotonicity from Section1 proves beta(t)<=1/2 for every T>=s*.

All hypotheses concern an actual individually centered section. The lemma does not assert that arbitrary centered laws reduce to that section, and it does not assert the all-dimensional lower or upper pointwise dual inequalities. Those remain separate obligations.
